issues.legal_issue: A private composition arrangement that postpones enforcement does not suspend limitation for executing a decree by analogy to the statutory exclusion for an injunction or court order.
material_facts: The decree-holders filed execution applications more than three years after their previous applications had been dismissed.
The creditors and debtors entered a composition arrangement providing for payment from property managed by trustees within a stated period, with a possible extension at the trustees’ discretion.
The insolvency court accepted the composition, but no injunction or court order stayed execution of the decrees during the payment period.
The judgment-debtor against whom execution was sought was not a party to the insolvency proceedings.
issues.conclusion: Section 15(1) of the Limitation Act, 1908 applies only where execution has been stayed by an injunction or order. The composition arrangement did not suspend limitation, and the execution applications were not saved from being time-barred by that arrangement.
issues.legal_principle: Section 15(1) of the Limitation Act, 1908 excludes the time during which execution is stayed by an injunction or order; it does not cover a private arrangement that merely delays enforcement. The Limitation Act is procedural and exhaustive, and its provisions cannot be extended by analogy to circumstances outside their express or necessary implication. The Court distinguished Govind Naik Gurunathnaik v. Basawannawa Parutappa, Pulin Chandra Sen v. Amin Mia Muzaffar Ahmad, Lakhan Chunder Sen v. Madhusudan Sen, Nrityamoni Dassi v. Lakhan Chandra Sen, Badruddin Khan v. Mahyar Khan, and Managing Committee Sundar Singh Malha Singh Rajput High School, Indore v. Sunder Singh Malha Singh Sanatan Dharma Rajput High School Trust.

rule.if: execution_application and private_composition_set_payment_period and no_court_order_stayed_execution and judgment_debtor_not_party_to_insolvency_proceeding

predicates.execution_application: A decree-holder seeks enforcement of a decree through an execution application.
predicates.private_composition_set_payment_period: The debtors and creditors entered a private composition that set a period for payment from property managed by trustees.
predicates.no_court_order_stayed_execution: No injunction or court order stayed execution of the decree during the composition payment period.
predicates.judgment_debtor_not_party_to_insolvency_: The judgment-debtor against whom execution was sought was not a party to the insolvency proceeding in which the composition was accepted.

issues.definition: When a decree is being enforced, a private composition setting a payment period does not suspend limitation where no court order stayed execution and the judgment-debtor was outside the insolvency proceeding.

issues.legal_issue: A debtor’s letter demanding that trustees discharge their separate obligations under a composition does not acknowledge the debtor’s own liability under a decree.
material_facts: The composition arrangement vested legal title to the property in trustees and made them responsible for paying creditors from that property, while the debtor’s liability under the decrees remained distinct.
The debtor, through counsel, sent the trustees a letter demanding payment of the debtor’s maintenance allowance and distribution of creditor dividends under the composition.
The letter did not refer to the decrees or to the debtor’s own liability under them.
issues.conclusion: The letter did not acknowledge the debtor’s liability within the meaning of section 19 of the Limitation Act, 1908, and did not extend the limitation period.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 19 of the Limitation Act, 1908, an acknowledgment must relate to a subsisting liability and, expressly or by implication, indicate an intention to admit the relevant jural relationship. A reference to a liability resting on another person is not an acknowledgment of the writer’s own liability. The Court applied the principles stated in Khan Bahadur Shapoor Freedom Mazda v. Durga Prosad Chamaria but held that case inapplicable because the letter here referred to the trustees’ distinct obligations, not the debtor’s liability under the decrees.

rule.if: execution_application and composition_created_distinct_trustee_obligation and letter_demands_trustee_performance and not letter_acknowledges_debtor_decree_liability

predicates.execution_application: A decree-holder seeks enforcement of a decree through an execution application.
predicates.composition_created_distinct_trustee_obl: The composition made trustees responsible for payments from property vested in them, separately from the debtor’s liability under the decree.
predicates.letter_demands_trustee_performance: The debtor, through counsel, sent the trustees a letter demanding performance of their payment obligations under the composition.
predicates.letter_acknowledges_debtor_decree_liabil: The debtor’s written statement expressly or implicitly admits the debtor’s own subsisting liability under the decree.

issues.definition: A letter demanding that trustees perform their separate payment obligations does not extend limitation by acknowledgment if it does not admit the debtor’s own decree liability.
